question: When you are caring for a very sick patient who cannot respond, what is your main job as their nurse?

options.A: Discharging the patient as quickly as possible
options.B: Focusing solely on medication administration schedules
options.C: Waiting for family members to make all clinical decisions
options.D: Acting as the patient's primary defense and surrogate voice

explanation: You've got this! Since very ill patients can't speak up for themselves, you become their voice and protector to make sure they get safe, complete care. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why is even a small, subtle change in one body system so risky for a critically ill patient?

options.A: It can quickly lead to multi-organ collapse and emergency
options.B: It only affects the specific organ without causing other issues
options.C: It means lab values are completely normal
options.D: It usually indicates that the patient is ready for discharge

explanation: Think of it like a house of cards—very sick patients have little backup energy, so a small glitch can rapidly cascade into a bigger emergency. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h1)

question: Which handy tool do nurses use to track changes in a patient's level of consciousness?
explanation: Great clinical instinct! The Glasgow Coma Scale gives us a quick, standard way to check eye, verbal, and motor responses. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h2)

question: Why do we measure strict intake and output (I&O) for a critically ill patient?

options.A: To determine how much food the patient likes to eat
options.B: To monitor kidney function and fluid balance status
options.C: To calculate the exact hospital bill for fluids used
options.D: To prevent the patient from feeling thirsty

explanation: Spot on! Tracking what goes in and out helps you catch early signs of fluid overload or kidney trouble before they become dangerous. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h2)

question: When giving total care to a very ill patient, what is your absolute top priority?

options.A: Maintaining airway patency and breathing efficiency
options.B: Providing a full bath every morning
options.D: Ensuring clean bed linens and fresh hospital gowns

explanation: Oxygen is king! Keeping the airway clear is always priority number one because without oxygen, nothing else matters. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h3)

question: You hear gurgling sounds and see thick secretions in an unconscious patient's mouth. What is your very first action?

options.A: Turn the patient flat on their back and offer water
options.B: Administer a sleeping pill to calm the patient down
options.C: Wait for the doctor to arrive before doing anything
options.D: Suction the airway to clear out the secretions

explanation: Brilliant! Gurgling means the airway is blocked. Grab that suction machine right away to help them breathe easy again. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h3)

question: What is a major risk of keeping a urinary catheter in place without strict sterile technique?

options.A: Rapid weight gain and fluid retention
options.B: Instant muscle atrophy in the legs

explanation: You got it. Catheters give bacteria a free highway straight into the bladder, which is why sterile technique is non-negotiable! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h4)

question: Why do doctors and nurses prefer early tube feeding (enteral nutrition) over IV nutrition for very ill patients when possible?

options.A: It tastes much better for unconscious patients
options.B: It keeps the gut mucosa healthy and prevents bacterial translocation
options.C: It is completely free of any potential complications
options.D: It requires no monitoring of blood sugar levels

explanation: Keeping the gut working keeps the bad bacteria where they belong! Using the stomach and intestines helps protect the whole body. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h4)

question: How often should you turn an immobile, very ill patient to protect their skin?
explanation: The golden rule of positioning! Turning patients every two hours takes the pressure off bony areas and stops bedsores before they start. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a benefit of giving a daily bed bath to a very ill patient?

options.A: Providing gentle touch and comfort to the patient
options.B: Permanently curing chronic underlying heart disease
options.C: Removing sweat and bacteria from the skin surface
options.D: Allowing the nurse to inspect the skin for early redness

explanation: Bed baths are amazing for hygiene, comfort, and skin checks, but they unfortunately can't fix chronic internal conditions like heart disease. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h5)

question: Why is it usually better to give pain meds on a regular schedule instead of waiting for the patient to ask?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for nursing assessments
options.B: It is cheaper for the hospital pharmacy department
options.C: It maintains a steady therapeutic level of pain relief
options.D: It stops the patient from ever sleeping deeply

explanation: Scheduled dosing keeps pain under control before it flares up, making the patient much more comfortable than a roller-coaster approach. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h6)

question: If a patient cannot speak, which physical sign might tell you they are in pain?

options.B: Low blood pressure and calm posture
options.D: Warm and dry skin on the hands

explanation: Spot on! When patients can't talk, their body speaks for them—look out for a fast heart rate (tachycardia) and tight, frowning facial expressions. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h6)

question: Why should you always talk to an unconscious patient before doing a procedure?

options.A: To wake the patient up immediately from a coma
options.B: To prove to the family that the nurse is working
options.C: Because hearing is the last sense to disappear
options.D: To maintain dignity and acknowledge their presence

explanation: Never lose sight of the person! Even if they can't answer, talking to them shows respect and preserves their human dignity. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h7)

question: How should you communicate updates to the worried family of a critically ill patient?

options.A: Giving all information through a written notebook only
options.B: Speaking very quickly so they do not interrupt
options.C: Using clear, simple language without heavy medical jargon
options.D: Refusing to answer questions until visiting hours end

explanation: Families under stress need kindness and clarity. Dropping heavy medical terms just confuses them—keep it simple and reassuring! [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h7)

question: When a patient reaches the end of life, what is the main focus of nursing care?

options.A: Restricting family visits to maintain strict silence
options.B: Trying aggressive new surgical procedures to cure them
options.C: Focusing only on lab values and medication charts
options.D: Ensuring a peaceful, pain-free, and dignified transition

explanation: When cure is no longer possible, comfort is everything. End-of-life care is all about peace, dignity, and pain control. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h8)

question: Why are advance directives so helpful in critical or end-of-life care?

options.A: They guarantee that the patient will recover fully
options.B: They guide medical treatment according to the patient's prior wishes
options.C: They eliminate all paperwork for the hospital staff
options.D: They give the doctor total control over all decisions

explanation: Advance directives let patients make their choices known ahead of time, taking the guesswork out of difficult situations. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T1#GNS221_U4_T1_h8)
